scene.title: PostgreSQL vs MongoDB for Event Sourcing
scene.subtitle: Relational consistency vs document flexibility in event-sourced architecture

answer.headline: PostgreSQL is generally preferred for strict data consistency in event sourcing, while MongoDB offers high flexibility for ingestion-heavy, schema-evolving workloads.
body: Event sourcing requires reliable storage of ordered immutable event streams. PostgreSQL handles this via relational tables that offer strict ACID guarantees, ensuring complex domain invariants are protected during event processing. Its robust indexing, JSONB support, and window functions make querying and projecting historical states highly performant and predictable, making it a standard choice for systems where business logic and relational integrity are paramount.

MongoDB is a strong contender when the primary need is high-throughput ingestion of varying event structures. Its document-oriented nature excels at handling polymorphic events without rigid schema migrations. However, managing strict consistency across multiple aggregate streams or complex relational projections requires more application-level logic compared to PostgreSQL’s native SQL support, which provides powerful transactional tools to handle these constraints out of the box.
caveats: Both databases now support ACID transactions, but PostgreSQL's implementation is traditionally more battle-tested for complex multi-table relationships.
Event sourcing performance is heavily dependent on index management and hardware; results will vary based on specific write volumes and projection complexity.

items.label: Choose PostgreSQL if
items.value: You need complex multi-table invariants and reliable SQL analytics.

items.label: Choose MongoDB if
items.value: Your event schemas evolve rapidly and you need high ingestion speed.

spotlight.label: Architectural priority defines the choice: choose PostgreSQL for complex domain rules, MongoDB for rapid iteration and high-velocity ingestion.
